items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We would go every night in Chicago—this was in the late ’40s—to hear Charlie Ventura and Jackie and Roy out on the South Side

ctx.x: I mentioned about some of the others. How did he feel about, and I just want to get a little bit of insight, because I know he was a very important influence on you as well, so this may eventually, this will tie in to what we’re saying, how is his feeling about swing music and about bebop or even more, say, more contemporary, like I say, did he hear Fats Navarro? Did he have any comments about Clifford Brown or Lee Morgan or some of the players that came up 20 years, 30 years after his time?

Yeah, but he was . . . he admitted that he was . . . he felt that he was committed to the style that he played. I think a lot of the . . . even sometimes with Dizzy, he would say, “It seems that all they do is play a lot of notes.” And yet when anybody would play a beautiful ballad or something, he would always dig that. I couldn’t hear him . . . he didn’t . . . I couldn’t see him getting into bebop. I think he had the style of playing so set in his mind that he wasn’t or couldn’t or wouldn’t change it. But at…
and he would play them. But his heart wasn’t in it. Yet he really admired other people. He loved Dizzy. Maybe more as a friend than . . .
